content.thinking:
Line counts match, so now I'm sketching the design: a red panda roughly 0.55m body, 0.45m tail, balanced atop a mossy rounded stone about 0.3m tall, with a forepaw lifted for balance.

I'm building the stone from a lumpy cluster of flat-shaded spheres, then adding moss tufts, tiny mushrooms, ferns, and glowing dendro-style motifs reminiscent of Genshin Impact — small green glowing seed motes or a glowing leaf-flower. For the panda itself, I'm considering a subtle gold-trimmed accessory, maybe a teal ribbon collar with a small gold dendro-glyph pendant, since a full hanging tassel wouldn't suit the simple silhouette.

I'm now laying out the skeleton structure: a spine chain from hips through neck to head, a tail chain, four leg chains, ears, jaw, and whisker elements, plus decal eyes. For positioning, I'm placing the stone top at y=0.26 and sizing the stone footprint to roughly 0.5m wide and deep to support the panda's body length of about 0.42m, then working out hip and shoulder joint coordinates along the spine for a chunky, rounded torso.

Now I'm roughing out leg proportions for a plantigrade stance and designing the head details—wide skull shape, cheek tufts, snout, large upright ears with white inner coloring, and the characteristic red panda facial markings like the white muzzle and eyebrow patches.

For coloring, I'm planning the paint functions to be defined relative to head-local coordinates since everything's built in rest pose, then choosing body colors: a vibrant rusty red-orange back, dark chocolate-black underside and legs to match red panda markings, and a ringed tail alternating between lighter and darker orange-red tones.

Now I'm working out the tail rig as a chain of six joints curving back and upward from the hips for balance, with a bushy taper from wide at the base to narrow and dark at the tip, plus cream-colored rings painted along its length and a white face with toon-style cel shading and fur edges separating the coat from the dark belly.

For texture I'm adding fur-tuft cards at the cheeks, ears, and tail tip using zigzag edges and a small orange teardrop texture, keeping the count limited for performance. For the pose, I'm deciding to keep all four paws planted on the stone with legs spread slightly apart and the tail raised in an S-curve for balance, favoring a neutral rig-friendly stance over a lifted paw, while treating the stone as a separate part attached to the root joint rather than part of the skeleton.

Now I'm working out the skeleton hierarchy: making a non-animated "base" joint at the origin to anchor the stone, with "hips" as its child acting as the first spine joint, then building out the spine chain from hips through additional named joints toward the chest.

Still working out joint naming...

Continuing on, I'm adding a jaw joint as a child of the head, plus ear joints under the head for sprouting ear shapes with hinge roles. Then for the front legs, I'm setting up shoulder socket positions and paw targets to build short limb chains appropriate for a red panda's proportions.

Now I'm working out the plantigrade front leg structure: three segments (upper arm, forearm, paw) with a sole direction so the paw sits flat, meaning the elbow bend direction points backward and the chain needs joint names for shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw across the resulting span points.

I'm also figuring out where the paw's sole contacts the ground, letting the paw tube sink slightly into the stone surface so the foot looks naturally planted rather than floating.

For the stone itself, I'm planning a flat-ish domed top so the paws make clean contact, building it as a jittered sphere geometry scaled into a squashed boulder shape, with vertex displacement adding lumpy, natural-looking irregularities.

I'll clamp the sphere's top to create a flat plateau at y0 for stable contact, and clamp the bottom so it sinks slightly into the floor — working out the center and radius values so the sphere spans the right range, settling on y0 = 0.27 with center at 0.15 and ry = 0.2.

This gives a mushroom-like boulder that's narrower at the base than at the plateau, widest around the middle — a nice natural rock shape with radial jitter for bumpiness. Now I'm planning to add a smaller companion rock, pebbles, moss tufts along the stone edges, ferns, mushrooms, and small glowing flowers for a Genshin-style touch.

I'm deciding on accessories for the panda: a gold-trimmed teal ribbon collar with a leaf pendant and glowing green gem plus tassel, skipping extra items like a tail ring or leaf hat to keep things clean.

For staging, I'm adding a low moss disc (radius ~0.5, barely raised off the ground) beneath the stone with grass tufts, since the tail extends behind and this ground patch will tie the whole diorama together.

Now I'm setting concrete dimensions, placing the plateau at y=0.27 and sweeping the torso along a spine path with varying radii from hips to chest to get that chonky stylized body shape, with a slight downward shift so the belly hangs naturally. I'm figuring out the fur edge paint pattern for the coat's color transition between rust and dark belly tones.

For the red panda coloring I'm using a lower edge level so the flanks darken toward the belly and legs, nesting that into the cel shading so the shadow tone derives from the resolved base color. I'm also considering adding fluffy fur tufts as cards at the cheeks, ear rims, tail edges, and back using a neutral white tuft texture that picks up tint from the part's color.

Now I'm sketching head details: a small scaled sphere for the skull with smooth cel shading, white tufted spheres for cheeks, a cream-white ellipsoid muzzle with a tiny dark nose sphere, and planning a separate lower jaw piece with its own joint.

For the eyes, I'm placing decals on the skull with warm amber-gold irises, sized fairly large for a cute stylized look, positioned symmetrically at a set azimuth and elevation on the head surface, and I'm considering adding white brow/cheek markings typical of red pandas.

Writing face paint logic...

Still defining tear-line markings...

Computing the ear mirroring and thickness vectors so the front faces outward correctly...

Setting up ear joints with hinge rotation at the base, then adding thin whisker sweeps (3 per side, cream colored) rigged to the head bone. For legs, I'm going with a dark cel-shaded tone with derived shadow colors and tiny claws on the paws.

For the paws themselves, I'm adding small toe bumps via tiny spheres plus cone-shaped cream claws at the tips, and widening the paw end of the limb sweep with an extra ellipsoid "mitten" shape for a chunkier look.

For hind legs, I'm setting up a three-segment chain with a sole—hip to knee to heel to toe—using plantigrade bends so the hock angles backward like a real red panda's hind leg, with the sole flag adjusting which joints bend.

Checking the overall proportions: body length roughly 0.45 plus head gets close to real red panda dimensions, but the leg segment lengths look too short relative to the hip height, meaning the legs would need to be quite bent to reach the ground realistically.

I want cute, slightly chibi-stylized proportions with a bigger head, in keeping with elegant Genshin character design. For the tail I'm plotting a chain of points curving up and back from the hips, but the total length comes out to about 0.7m, longer than a real red panda's bushy 0.45-0.5m tail, so I'll need to shorten it.

Shortening the tail chain to about 0.55-0.6m total, letting it curve upward for balance even though it extends slightly past the stone's edge. I'm sizing the tail rings to be thicker in the middle and tapering at the tip, and planning the coloring with alternating rust and creamy-orange bands with a darker tip to match a real red panda's coat.

Now I'm adding zigzag-edged ring patterns in rust and lighter orange tones with slight oblique wobble for texture, darkening the last twelve percent of the tail tip to brown, and scattering small fluff cards across the tail surface for extra fuzziness without adding too many triangles. For the neck and head, I'm connecting the chest to the head base with a short thick curved segment.

Now I'm settling on the color palette: rust with a darker red-shadow variant, dark plum for belly and legs with a deeper shadow, cream with a warm tan shadow, teal ribbon accented with gold and a bronze shadow, and a bluish-grey stone tone for any stylized rock elements.

I'm also planning the moss placement logic — distributing moss across the stone based on surface normal and noise so flatter, upward-facing areas get mossy while sides stay patchier, with the plateau the panda stands on being fully covered. I want to add moss tufts and hanging drips along the plateau edges using card-based clumps textured like green blobs, scattered across the stone surface using noise.

I'm sketching small decorative life for the scene: little mushroom clusters near the stone base, fern cards, and white flowers with gold centers dotting the ground. For glow effects, I'm thinking of floating dendro-seed particles drifting with a soft green glow and gold ring accents, plus a glowing gem for the pendant. Then I move to the collar — sweeping a teal ribbon loop around the neck joint — and start designing a gold leaf-shaped pendant with a glowing gem and tassel.

I'm deciding to keep the accessories balanced: a collar with pendant and tassel, a gold ring-band at the tail base with a small tassel, and a leaf tucked behind the ear for extra flair, rather than overloading with wrist bands too. For the pendant, I'm extruding a beveled leaf shape in gold with a glowing gem at its center and small gold beads arranged around the rim for a filigree effect.

For surrounding scene details, I'm planning simple decorative cards like fur tufts, moss clumps, grass blades, and tassels, keeping the color palette limited and cel-shaded. I'm also designing a lumpy ground disc beneath the stone using a lathe profile with a mossy green painted texture, making sure the stone base sinks slightly into the disc so the contact point looks natural.

Now I'm tallying up the joint hierarchy: a base joint, spine chain, neck, head, jaw, ears, four-jointed legs on each side, and a six-point tail using a catmull spline, totaling roughly 35 joints with no extra joints needed for the tassel charm.

Front legs parent off the chest spine joint while hind legs parent off the hips, and I'm checking that chain side-detection works by confirming the first joint's x-coordinate is nonzero. For the body, I'll sweep a tube along the spine chain alone, letting the neck get its own separate sweep that joins seamlessly at the chest cap since the radii are close enough, and I'm placing the root base joint at the floor center so the stone geometry can parent to it correctly.

For the head, I'm positioning whisker and eye decals using spherical coordinates around the head center, with the mirror flag flipping left-right placement, then sizing and positioning the muzzle and nose spheres slightly below and in front of the head center to give the face its cute, rounded shape.

Thinking through the red panda's facial coloring, I'm mapping out the white around the muzzle and lower cheeks against the rust-colored top of the head, computing local offsets from head center to determine where cream patches transition from rust, using a zigzag boundary threshold for the cheek line beneath the eyes.

I notice the eye decal size is overlapping with the brow patch I'm trying to place above it — I need to shrink the eye dimensions down to around .032 by .043 so there's clear separation between the eye region and the narrower cream brow stripe sitting just above it.

I'm also adding dark tear line markings running from under each eye down to the mouth corners, using a rust-brown color that overrides the cream base, and thinking about bumping the overall skull scale slightly larger before iterating in preview. Then I'm working through how the cel-shading wrapper interacts with the lit paint function, since the paint resolution logic needs to correctly pass through colors based on the surface normal.

For the jaw area, I'm adding a small cream ellipsoid beneath the muzzle for the lower jaw, and considering whether to add a thin ink decal for the mouth line and philtrum rather than modeling actual geometry—sketching a W-shaped sweep that could be draped onto the muzzle surface or applied as an SVG decal instead.

I'm also deciding the mouth decal should be an ink "w" stroke with a tiny pink tongue accent, weighted to follow the head bone. For the back, I'm weighing whether to add subtle fur color variation (lighter crown, darker red-brown back) with an ink furEdge line marking the belly boundary, and wondering if similar ink tooth-edge lines should separate the moss and stone textures.

I'm sketching the moss/stone blend logic using layered noise and a zigzag pattern to decide moss placement relative to a threshold, plus adding darker crack lines through the stone using cell noise where adjacent cell distances are close. Since the stone is low-poly with per-face normals, I'm considering switching from normal-based moss placement to position-based blending with noise so the moss patches don't look overly faceted.

I'm also working out texture resolution needs — estimating total painted surface area across the stone and other parts to figure out texel density, concluding a 1024 paint resolution should be sufficient given roughly 600 texels per meter.

Beyond texturing, I'm now designing the glowing dendro-seed motes floating around the scene — small octahedron shapes in glowing green, plus fireflies and maybe a thin gold ring orbiting the pendant for extra sparkle.

For the tail charm, I'm placing a gold ring at a joint with a tassel hanging from it, using a card setup with lean and flow parameters to make the tassel drape naturally given the tail's horizontal posture. Then I want to decorate the stone base itself with moss tufts, hanging moss strands, and small painted mushrooms for extra environmental detail.

For the mushrooms, I'll give them warm orange caps with dotted spots and plain white stems, plus scatter in tiny flat pebbles and simple daisy-like flowers made from stem-and-bloom card textures standing upright for a flat, stylized look.

Now I'm planning to scatter flower, grass, and fern cards across the ground disc surface by filtering raycast hits where the normal points mostly upward, giving that lush Genshin-style ground cover, with the cards rooted at the base joint. I'm starting to sketch the SVG shapes for these, beginning with a flame-like white tuft shape anchored at the card's bottom edge.

Writing moss, grass, and fern textures...

Since hanging cards get flipped when viewed from below, I realize I need to invert the tassel drawing: the gold cap goes at the bottom of the SVG with strands flaring upward, since the attachment point ends up on top once hung.

Now I'm sketching the mouth SVG with a path for the philtrum and curved lines forming the upper lip on each side.

I'm also deciding whether the nose needs its own decal piece, placing it on the muzzle sphere facing outward, and tuning the eye colors with warm amber iris, a lighter highlight, and skipping blush for a more animal-like look while keeping a subtle brow line.

Setting up imports for the build: math helpers, path utilities, limb/IK, paint and toon rendering functions for the fur, eyes, and ink outlines.

Now I'm writing a custom stone geometry generator—deforming a sphere's vertices with layered sine noise to create lumpy rock bumps, then clamping the height to stay within a flat plateau range.

Plateau extends through 45°, and the ring at 67.5° sits just below it, creating a steep transition between the flattened top and the sloping sides below—giving the overall rounded, boulder-like shape I'm after.

I'll clamp the bottom so it flattens instead of pinching to a point, and shift the shape slightly off-center so it doesn't read as too symmetrical. Now I'm writing the stone's paint function, blending noise with a zigzag pattern to create mossy edge variation across the surface.

Still writing paint logic...

Adding mottled fur variation and edge shading for the body...

Legs should be dark solid, blending into the body with subtle gradients at the shoulders—matching the brown-black tones of real red panda legs. For the tail, I'm writing a zigzag ring pattern function that uses chain position and tip darkening to create the characteristic striped tail look.

Now I'm thinking about fluff tufts for cheeks and chest, using a cream tone like "#fff1dc" for cheeks against the grey-white fur and a rust tone like "#f07a32" for body tufts, shaded along the frame's normal axis.

For claws I'm adding three small cream spikes at each paw's toe tip, spawning them from the leg chain's end joint with a short forward-pointing offset and slight downward angle, using the tip joint directly as the bone reference.

Thinking about toe nubs—maybe tiny light-colored spheres near the claws for visual separation—but the paw capsule sweep probably covers that detail well enough on its own. I'm also considering adding small gold wrist bands as Genshin-style ornamentation, looping a thin gold sweep around the wrist joint, though I'm wary of the loop cut missing the surface and throwing an error.

I decide to limit the gold accents to three locations: front wrist bracelets, a neck collar, and a tail ring, skipping the hind ankles for simplicity. For the collar, I'm placing a loop cut at the midpoint of the neck sweep, using a frame oriented along the neck's tangent so the cut plane faces forward—though I need to watch for overlap issues where the neck tube meets the chest sphere's cap region.

For the collar sweep itself, I'm settling on a thin teal ribbon shape with a small rectangular cross-section, using a flat teal color or cel-shaded paint for visual consistency with the gold cel style elsewhere. Then I'm positioning the pendant at the lowest point of the collar loop, figuring out the angle convention where zero is "up" and the loop runs counterclockwise so the pendant naturally hangs at the belly-facing low point.

Working out the exact frame orientation for the hanging leaf pendant now, choosing axis directions so the extrude's thickness vector points correctly out of the plane, computing the cross product of the chosen x and y directions to confirm it faces the right way.

I'm now designing the leaf outline as a teardrop shape with a smoothed point at the bottom, attached at the top, and adding a small glowing green gem embedded near the base of the leaf.

Thinking through attachment: I need to anchor the pendant to a bone near the neck so it hangs rigidly from the front of the collar, letting it fall over the chest when the head tilts forward.

Checking the geometry, though, I realize the pendant's position at the neck's underside is only about .061 units from the chest sphere's center, which is less than the chest radius of .075 — meaning the pendant would actually be buried inside the chest sphere rather than resting on its surface.

I need to move the collar point forward to roughly z=.24, placing it closer to the head's base. Recalculating the distance there puts the pendant leaf just outside the chest sphere, but now I'm worried about the head radius overlapping the neck region since the neck segment is quite short, so I'm considering restructuring the spine chain to lengthen the neck and shift the chest and head joint positions accordingly.

Instead of having the pendant partly embedded in fur, I'll cast a ray from the front of the chest to find the correct surface hit point, place the pendant slightly offset outside that surface, and connect it to the collar with a cord sweep from the collar bottom to the pendant top.

Checking the geometry, the collar needs to sit where the neck radius exceeds the chest sphere's shrinking cap radius—otherwise it gets buried inside the chest mesh. I'll thicken the neck slightly and add more fur ruff for a cuter look, placing the collar further up where the proportions work out.

Now I'm plotting the neck curve as it ascends toward the head joint, and setting the head center position so the muzzle extends forward appropriately given the body proportions.

Checking overall scale: total height comes out to roughly .6 above the stone, which feels right. The skull proportions at .176 wide read as chunky-stylized compared to a real red panda's narrower head, while the body length and girth both land close to realistic reference measurements.

Shrinking the skull slightly to balance the chibi head-to-body ratio better. For the hind legs, I'm working out the hip-to-ankle geometry — the socket sits almost directly above the foot placement, so the knee needs to bend forward to account for the limb segment lengths, with a longer hind paw than the front.

For the front legs, I'm checking shoulder-to-wrist positioning so the paws land on the ground without overlapping the head or chin, and since the upper arm and forearm lengths nearly span the straight-line distance, the elbow bend needs to angle backward.

Spreading legs slightly for balance, with front legs a bit wider than hind legs given the body width, and settling on a naming convention where side sign maps to left/right joint labels. I'm also planning a reusable leg-building helper function and making sure the hip-to-base bone chain connects properly before moving into the spine.

I'm varying the body cross-section radius along the spine using sine-based interpolation between hips, mid-body, and chest, plus a slight downward shift for belly sag, then sweeping the coat-colored body mesh along that spine chain with rounded caps. For the haunches, I'm adding ellipsoid thigh masses at each hip joint to give the hindquarters more volume.

Now I'm thinking about shading the thigh rust above and dark below to match a red panda's coloring, adding similar shoulder ellipsoid blobs for plumpness, and then moving on to positioning the ears using local coordinates projected forward and outward from the head joint.

For the ears, I'm setting up a mirrored loop so left and right ears share the same geometry but flip sign on the sideways offset, then sketching an extruded outline for a rounded, slightly pointed ear shape using a small set of smoothed points.

Now I'm working out the tilt direction for each ear so they angle outward from the head, checking that the cross product of the local axes still points forward correctly.

Computing cross product confirms the x-direction stays consistent and the ear outline remains symmetric for both orientations. Now I'm working out the ear paint pattern, defining an inner cream region bordered by rust within the extruded shape.

Scattering tufts along the skull sides with sweeping back-and-down flow for a natural fur direction, plus a forehead ruff tuft. Then I'm placing a gold ring near the tail base with a loop around the tail path for the tassel detail.

Moving to dressing: the painted stone itself, a lathed mossy-grass ground disc sized to clear the tail, two small boulders scattered with varied seeds plus pebbles, and now moss card scatter filtered to the plateau where the panda stands.

Adding hanging moss on the stone's sides, plus grass, fern, and flower cards scattered across the ground while keeping clear of the tail's air zone, and masking out the area under the stone with an elliptical distance filter so disc scatter doesn't poke through. Next I'm planning mushroom clusters built from lathed caps and swept stems.

I'll place mushrooms at radius .3 hugging the stone's base near ground level, and maybe a small cluster near the panda's legs. Then I still need flower cards/daisies scattered on the ground, plus around eight floating glow motes positioned around the panda.

For the dendro seed glow I'm using a tiny elongated octahedron with green shading, surrounded by small motes sized .008-.014 and a scatter of tiny leaf-shaped cards built from extruded outlines, tilted and floating near the seed for a magical glimmer effect.

I'm placing a couple of leaf accessories near the left ear, one scaled up and tilted at the base with a gold stem, plus a small gold hair-clip bead to tie in the teal/gold color accents. For whiskers I'm sketching thin cream sweeps, three per side, curving outward from the muzzle with a narrow radius for a delicate look.

I'm skipping the eyebrow patches and teeth for now, but I am building out the jaw: a small cream-toned lower jaw sphere positioned under the muzzle, hinged forward from a jaw bone anchored near the head's local coordinates, with the muzzle itself defined as a scaled sphere offset downward and forward from the head center.

Since the skull sphere is large enough to cover most of the jaw area, I decide a visible jaw sliver is acceptable without needing a separate mouth interior -- a closed mouth with a decal works fine. I'm placing the nose as a small flattened dark sphere near the muzzle tip, with a tiny white highlight dot for a touch of cuteness.

Checking the eye placement against the muzzle, I'm sizing eyes around .036×.05 to get that larger anime-style look while tolerating slight overlap with the muzzle edge, and I'm considering adding a darker rust-brown patch around each eye to mimic a red panda's natural eye markings.

I'll skip toon-style rim outlines since the geometry only renders from the front, and instead focus on a simpler ink line along the belly seam, plus dark coloring for the legs and claws before moving to write the actual code.

Building the joint hierarchy...

Still defining jaw joint and head-local helper point...

Writing leg-generation code...

Writing sweep radii and claw spikes...

I should verify the leg reach with a quick preview and typecheck run. For the thigh, I'll add a blob sphere scaled and offset at the hip, shaded darker underneath based on normal direction and rustier on top. For the tail, I'm setting up a bone chain with six segments parented to the spine, naming each joint sequentially.

For the tail shape, I'll vary the radius along its length so it's thicker in the middle and tapers toward the tip, with rounded caps and maybe a slight zigzag for a fluffy edge. Then I'll scatter around fifty tuft cards along the tail and add a teal ribbon and gold ring accent, followed by texturing the collar pendant tassel, wrist bands, and ground disc placement.

For the ground disc, I'll use a lathed base shape painted with a mossy green mottle pattern and lighter dots, using a cel-shaded lighting approach so the top stays flat-lit with an inked ring edge. To make it feel more organic than a perfect lathe, I'm considering building a lumpy, jittered disc geometry similar to the stone approach, just flattened.

Actually I want the rim to sit right at the floor, so the equator of the disc should be at y=0 instead of below it — I'm reworking the geometry so the widest point clamps at the floor level with the top rounding off a bit higher.

For the general rock shape, I'm generalizing the lumpy geometry function so both big stones and small rocks share parameters: a center height, radius variations per axis, clamped top and bottom, plus a `flat` option. I'm also generalizing the stone paint function to take a top-Y value and moss depth so I can reuse it for pebbles with their own smaller flattened-sphere geometry.

Now I'm figuring out how to keep card textures lean -- grouping tufts, cheeks, tails, moss, grass, ferns, and flowers by material, deciding which stay grey (and get tinted per-card by color) versus which keep their own drawn colors.

Writing SVG code...

Still writing moss shapes...

For grass I'm drawing a few curved blades in varying greens, and for the fern I'm building a curving stem with rows of small leaflet ellipses generated by a loop, scaling the size up so the stroke width stays visible.

Now I'm sketching the flower icon with a thin stem and leaf, then arranging six white petals with a golden center, scaled up 4x for the final size. For the tassel I'm adding teal strand paths, a gold bead at the bottom, a neck band, and a skirt shape to complete the decorative look.

I also need a mouth decal SVG and a reusable leaf-outline function, plus deciding on sizing ratios and color choices for a floating leaf element with a gold midrib.

For scattering details, I'm working out moss tuft placement on stone surfaces and ground patches using filtered scatter hits based on normal direction and distance, plus setting tail card flow, bend, and lean for a warm tinted color.

Now I'm figuring out the gold wrist band placement — deciding whether to loop around the wrist joint, elbow joint, or an interpolated point along the chain, since the wrist's bone direction points forward along the paw rather than the forearm, which would cut the wrong part of the limb.

I'm figuring out the ribbon's box-section sweep with a teal color, then working out where the pendant cord attaches — it should hang from the collar's bottom point, which I can find at t=.5 along the loop path since it starts facing up and runs opposite at the halfway point.

Now I'm placing the pendant itself just below that collar point, extruding it with a bone binding to the neck joint, and adding a tassel hanging further down with its own frame and lean orientation — though I'm wary this might overlap the chest piece, so I'll need to check in preview. I'm also setting up a tail ring along the tail path and figuring out where its tassel should hang from the ring's bottom point.

Now I'm defining the facial paint markings on the head using a procedural function based on distance from the head center, computing tear-streak lines running from the eye corner down to the mouth corner using a linear interpolation, plus cheek cream patches defined by a zigzag edge threshold depending on depth and horizontal position.

I'm also setting up a brow band, an eye patch defined using an elliptical distance formula, and a mottled rust crown for the top of the head, while settling on a layering order (tear over cream over brow over patch over rust) so overlapping regions resolve correctly.

Defining more colors...

I'm keeping the flat color palette small, under the 64-color limit, while using paint materials for shared parts. Now I'm writing a helper function to generate lumpy organic geometry with configurable radius, seed, and amplitude parameters.

Still writing geometry function...

Now I'm placing ferns near the rocks via scatter with a distinct rng to avoid overlap with the stone, then planning the overall scene metadata—name, description, style tag—before committing. I'm also setting positions for floating motes scattered around the panda.

Adjusting mote heights so nothing floats above the panda's silhouette, then adding a few floating leaves with flat-shaded octahedron geometry for a glowing effect. Working out the orientation vectors for the floating leaves so they tilt naturally using cross products between an upward-ish random direction and the up vector.

Writing orientation helper...

Whiskers get cream-colored tapered sweeps with a point cap, skipping teeth and tongue detail since there's no cute alternative for them. For texture I'm scattering tufts across the dorsal body and cheek regions using filtered card placements tinted rust, keeping the skull smooth where sweeps already define the shape.

Now I'm composing everything together, placing cards on the spine sweep surface and double-checking the chain builder's naming parameter works for the six-segment tail. I'm also auditing imports to make sure only the paint, toon, and type helpers actually used in the final code are included, typing outline arrays inline rather than pulling in extra types.
